name: Bulguksa
label: Bulguksa Temple
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/382655135: large area 'Bulguksa Temple' (614 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Famous UNESCO-listed Silla temple on Mount Toham.

text.description:
Bulguksa is a large Buddhist temple on the slopes of Tohamsan, and it is the most rewarding stop on this map. The site is made up of stone terraces, timber halls and gates, so there is something to photograph in almost every direction. The best-known subjects are the entrance stairway with its two bridges, Cheongungyo (Blue Cloud Bridge) and Baegungyo (White Cloud Bridge), which together have 34 steps. Beyond them are the two pagodas in the main courtyard. Dabotap is 10.4 metres tall and richly carved. Seokgatap is 8.2 metres tall and much plainer, and the contrast between the two makes a good pair of photos.

The records say the present temple was begun in 751 and finished in 774. The wooden buildings were burned during the Imjin wars and rebuilt later, with a major restoration between 1969 and 1973. The famous stonework is preserved from the original Silla construction. Bulguksa and nearby Seokguram Grotto were added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1995.

For your phone, work with the shapes: the diagonal of the stairway, the pagodas against the hall behind them, and the rooflines. Take a wide shot first to show the setting, then move closer for carved details. Keep people out of the frame by waiting a few seconds between groups. The Lotus Flower Bridge and Seven Treasures Bridge, a smaller pair to the west, are closed to walkers, so photograph them from where you can see them.
text.geographic_location: Bulguksa stands on the slopes of Tohamsan in Jinhyeon-dong, Gyeongju, North Gyeongsang Province.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stops are listed for this spot, so make your way to Bulguksa Temple in Jinhyeon-dong, Gyeongju. The phone icon on the map is about 20 m west of the numbered pin. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the stairway, gate and courtyard, where the buildings are close and fill the frame. Use the default lens (1x) for most general shots, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for pagoda carvings and roof details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 20 m west of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line a pagoda or a hall column up with a vertical line so the stonework does not lean. Frame Dabotap and Seokgatap in separate shots first, then try one wider shot with both in it. For the stairway, crouch slightly and let the steps lead the eye up to the gate.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the pale stone to focus, then pull the exposure slider down a little so the sky and stone keep their detail. Use portrait mode only for people, not for the buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go early in the morning or later in the afternoon, when there are usually fewer visitors in your shots and the light is softer.

text.access_note: This is a working temple and a heritage site, so check the official site before you go for opening times and entry details, and dress and behave respectfully inside.

photo.from: Own photo, taken 18 m from the phone icon

name: Seokguram
label: Seokguram Grotto
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '석굴암전망대' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: '석굴암' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/372401044: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Seokguram Grotto' (17 m across).
notes: UNESCO-listed grotto with a Buddha statue on Mount Toham.

text.description: Seokguram is a small hermitage and granite grotto high on Tohamsan, about 3 kilometres from Bulguksa and part of the same World Heritage listing (1995). Work began in 751 and finished in 774, in the Unified Silla period. It sits around 750 metres above sea level and looks out towards the East Sea. For a phone photographer the setting is the main draw. Photography is not allowed inside the grotto, so every picture has to be taken from outside. The lookout is a terrace on the approach with a wide view over the ridges of Tohamsan and out towards the distant sea. The grotto area is close by, which gives the view some context. The same guide describes it as a good place for memorial shots. Check on arrival what you can see of the grotto from the lookout. For a second frame, walk on to the stairs in front of the grotto's wooden entrance building. From there you can shoot it straight on, with the stone-stepped approach leading up to it. Take your time on the walk, as the road is winding and trail work has been reported on the path.
text.geographic_location: Seokguram is on the slopes of Tohamsan above Gyeongju, about 3 kilometres from the Bulguksa temple complex. The lookout is on the Seokguram approach, close to the grotto area.
text.directions_text: No train or tram stops are listed nearby, so start from Bulguksa and take the bus or the forest trail to Seokguram. The road is winding and the trail may have work in progress, so check current conditions. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the main view of the lookout and ridges. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in more of the mountains, or to the telephoto (2x-5x on many phones) to pick out the ridge lines and the sea in the distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on 석굴암전망대 (on the Seokguram approach, near the grotto area (address 석굴로 238)). A lookout over Tohamsan's mountain ridges and the distant East Sea, with the grotto area nearby for context. The grotto area lies a short way to the west, so turn that way for context, and check on arrival whether the grotto building fits in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower third line. Use the ridges as layers leading to the sea. For a memorial shot, ask someone to take a photo of you at 1x with the view behind. For a second angle, go to the stairs in front of the grotto entrance and shoot the wooden building straight on with the stone steps leading up to it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the ridges to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little if the sky looks washed out. Try panorama mode for the full sweep of the mountains, and hold the phone steady as you pan slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late morning, when a guide says the sun lights the grotto entrance directly. Sunrise over the sea is also popular, but check the official site for current visiting times before you go.

text.access_note: Seokguram is a Buddhist hermitage and heritage site where photography is not allowed inside the grotto, so check the official site before you go for current access and visiting rules.

name: Cheomseongdae
label: Cheomseongdae
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '계림' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '경주 계림' (way/382133881): middle (370 m across).
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-17: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Ancient Silla stone observatory, one of the oldest in Asia.

text.description:
Cheomseongdae is a small stone tower in Gyeongju that was built as an observatory, and it is thought to be the oldest surviving one in Asia. It dates from the Silla period, in the reign of Queen Seondeok (632–647). It is only 9.17 metres high, but the shape is easy to spot: a square base, a gently curved bottle-like body of 27 tiers of granite, and a square frame on top. A square window opens on the south side. The body is made of 365 cut stones, which is usually taken to stand for the days of the year. The tower leans very slightly to the north-east, and it became a national treasure in 1962.

From the wooded path you look back toward the tower through the trees. The setting is shadier and usually quieter than the open lawn in front of it. In autumn a cosmos path can frame the view. If you want the classic view, the tower rises over the lawn with seasonal flowers in front. Pink muhly grass in autumn works well for a low-angle shot. The flowers change through the year, with tulips in April, then cherry blossom, sunflowers in summer, and pink muhly and cosmos in autumn. Climbing the tower is not allowed, and visitors report that staff ask people to keep off the grass.
text.geographic_location: Cheomseongdae is in Gyeongju, South Korea, and is part of the Gyeongju Historic Areas World Heritage Site.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or station stop is listed for this spot, so head for central Gyeongju and walk or use local transport to 계림 (the wooded park a few minutes' walk from the observatory). Follow the wooded path toward it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the trees and the tower together. Try telephoto (2x or 3x, depending on your phone) to bring the tower closer between the trunks. The ultra-wide (0.5x) is useful only for the lawn and flower beds at the tower itself.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in 계림 (wooded path a few minutes' walk from the observatory, looking back toward the tower). Trees or a cosmos path framing the observatory from a quieter, more shaded angle. The photo shows trees, or a cosmos path in season, framing the observatory from a quieter, shadier angle than the main lawn.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Use the tree trunks or branches as a natural frame, and keep the tower roughly in the centre with gridlines switched on so it stands straight. For a different view, walk to the lawn in front of the tower and shoot low, with seasonal flowers in the foreground. In autumn the pink muhly area is a good alternative.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the pale stone keeps its detail against the sky. If the tower is dark among the trees, tap it again and nudge the slider up.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunny afternoons suit the cosmos-and-forest combination in autumn. Peak season brings crowds in front of the tower, so the wooded side is the calmer choice.

text.access_note: Climbing the tower is prohibited and drone flying typically needs prior approval, so check the official site for current rules before you go.

photo.artist: by Junho Jung at Flickr from South Korea

name: Woljeonggyo
label: Woljeong Bridge
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '징검다리' (4 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/539995254: the middle of the OpenStreetMap line '월정교' (68 m long).
notes: Restored wooden bridge over the Namcheon stream, lit at night.

text.description:
Woljeonggyo is a long wooden covered bridge across the Namcheon Stream, with a tiled roof and a gate pavilion at each end. It was first built in 760 A.D., in the Unified Silla period, and was later lost. The bridge you see now was rebuilt and opened in April 2018, with the gatehouses finished in the second phase of work. The rebuilt span is a little over 66 metres long. It is lit at night and is considered scenic then.

It works well on a phone because the whole structure fits in one frame. From the stepping stones (징검다리) directly in front of the bridge you can take in both gate pavilions, the long roofline and the reflection in the water, with the stones giving you a foreground. Take your first shot there with the default lens (1x), then move closer or step back to change the balance between bridge and water.

The stones can be slippery, so avoid them when the water is high or fast. If in doubt, take the same view from the bank. Two other views are worth a look. One is from the path along the stream bank, which shows the bridge's length side-on. The other is from inside the bridge itself, looking through the wooden pillars at the painted details. The upper floors of the gatehouses hold exhibits on how the bridge was rebuilt.
text.geographic_location: Woljeonggyo crosses the Namcheon Stream in Gyeongju, South Korea. The stepping stones sit on the stream directly in front of the bridge.
text.directions_text: Check the route on a map and head to Woljeonggyo on the Namcheon Stream. Once at the bridge, walk down to the stream bank and look for the stepping stones, which are the phone icon on the map. It sits at the middle of the bridge's length, on the stepping stones in front of the bridge. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x), which shows the whole bridge and its reflection from the stepping stones. If you are close and cannot fit both gate pavilions in, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x). Use the telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for roof tiles and painted details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the photo shows the full lit bridge with both gate pavilions, the tiled roof and the reflection in the water, with the stones in the foreground. Only go out on the stones if they are dry and the water is low. Otherwise stay on the bank.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the bridge along the upper third, leaving the lower part for the water and its reflection. Use the nearest stones as a leading line. Keep the phone level so the roofline stays straight. For a different view, try the path along the stream bank for a side-on shot of the bridge's length, or shoot from inside the bridge through the wooden pillars.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the bridge to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the lights do not wash out. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows on something steady, as the longer exposure blurs if you move. A Live Photo can help if people walk through the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Blue hour, when the sky still has some colour and the bridge lights are on.

text.access_note: The bridge is an outdoor public landmark, but opening times vary and the gatehouse interiors may close earlier, so confirm locally before you go.

name: Anapji
label: Donggung & Wolji (Anap
camera_source: Commons cluster (11 photos). Moved 142 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 15 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/477417220: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Donggung Palace and Wolji Pond' (429 m across).
notes: Silla palace pond, especially beautiful lit up at night.

text.description: Anapji, now known as Donggung Palace and Wolji Pond, is a Silla-era artificial pond that was part of the palace complex in central Gyeongju. King Munmu had it built in 674 CE. It is an oval about 200 m east to west and 180 m north to south, with three small islands, so there is plenty of shoreline and open water to frame. Walking the edge, you get a changing mix of water, trees, islands and reconstructed timber buildings. Excavation here between 1975 and 1986 turned up almost 33,000 relics, from roof tiles to gilt bronze Buddha figures. About 730 of them are shown in the Anapji Exhibition Hall at the Gyeongju National Museum. Imhaejeon, the building used as the crown prince's palace, is part of the grounds. Some parts have been rebuilt, while others have been left in a more natural state, which gives you a good contrast of tidy architecture and softer planting. For phone photos, go for the whole scene first, then step in for details. Keep the water in the lower part of the frame so the reflections and the pavilion rooflines both have room. Look for the curved shoreline and islands as natural lines leading the eye across the pond. Take a few frames as you walk round, as the view changes a lot.
text.geographic_location: Anapji lies in Inwang-dong, in central Gyeongju, at the north-east edge of the former Wolseong Palace site. It is part of Gyeongju National Park.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from central Gyeongju and head to the pond at the north-east edge of the old Wolseong Palace area. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole pond and its islands, then use the default lens (1x) for a natural view. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for roof details and the islands.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (Facing the third restored pavilion, reached by walking clockwise from the entrance). The palace pavilions mirrored head-on in the pond, the classic symmetrical reflection shot, most striking after dark.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the shoreline on a lower third line, with buildings or trees on the upper line. Use the curve of the bank or an island as a line leading into the picture. Try a second shot at 2x to pick out a single roof against the trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of the scene to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky and any lights do not wash out. In low light, hold the phone steady against your body or a rail and let night mode do its work.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or around dusk usually gives softer light and calmer water for reflections. Check the official site before you go for current visiting arrangements.

text.access_note: This is a managed heritage site within Gyeongju National Park, so access arrangements may apply; check the official site before you go.

name: Gyeongju National Museum
label: National Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/573218888: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Gyeongju National Museum' (588 m across).
notes: Silla gold crowns and the Divine Bell of King Seongdeok.

text.description:
The Gyeongju National Museum is the place to see what the Silla kingdom left behind. Gyeongju was Silla's capital, and the collection is largely devoted to that period. It holds several Silla crowns and the Emille Bell, which legend says rings with the voice of a child sacrificed in its casting. There are also finds from Anapji Pond and from the Hwangnyongsa Temple site. The museum began in 1945 as a branch of the National Museum of Korea, the main building went up in 1968, and it took its present name in 1975. It has been expanding ever since.

For a phone photographer the grounds are the draw. Many pieces are displayed outdoors, so you can photograph them in open air without fighting glass reflections. The site is large, so walk around and look for a clear view of a building front, an outdoor display piece against sky, or a path leading the eye in. The museum is next to the royal tomb complex, in an area that also includes the Gyerim forest, Cheomseongdae and Anapji Pond, so the trees and open space nearby make a pleasant backdrop. Stand a few steps back, keep the phone level, and let the building fill the frame. Indoor rules on photography can differ from room to room, so look for signs and ask staff if unsure.
text.geographic_location: The museum is in Gyeongju, right next to the royal tomb complex. The Gyerim forest, Cheomseongdae observatory, Banwolseong palace site and Anapji Pond are all in the same area.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. The museum is next to the royal tomb complex, so that is a good place to head for, in an area that also includes Cheomseongdae and Anapji Pond. Look for the Gyeongju National Museum (국립경주박물관) once you are in the area. Once there, the phone icon on the map is in the middle of the museum grounds. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for most views. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for the long building fronts and open grounds. Use 2x or more for details on outdoor display pieces.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. It sits in the middle of the museum grounds, so the museum is all around you rather than in one direction. Walk a little way from it until the building or piece you want fits the frame, then turn back to take the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the building edges with them so the walls look straight. Put an outdoor display piece in the foreground and the museum behind it for a sense of scale. Leave some sky at the top. If the day is busy, wait a moment for a gap in the crowd.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the display piece or building to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is washing out. Use portrait mode only for close pieces with a plain background. Check any rules about photography indoors before you take the phone out.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon, when the sun is lower and the light on outdoor display pieces is softer. Weekday mornings are likely to be quieter.

text.access_note: The museum is a public institution with indoor galleries and outdoor displays, so check the official site before you go for opening times, entry rules and photography rules.

name: Gyeongju Tower
label: Gyeongju Tower
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Gyeongju Tower'.
notes: Hwarang-inspired tower with views over the city.

text.description:
Gyeongju Tower is an observation tower in Gyeongju Expo Park, and it makes a clean, simple subject for a phone photo. It stands 82 metres tall, which is comparable to a 30-storey apartment block. It was completed on 14 August 2007, together with the Gyeongju Expo Culture Center.

Because the tower is tall and slim, the main challenge is fitting all of it in. From the phone icon on the map it sits right at your position, so you will be looking up at it from close range. Tilt the phone upwards and the sides will lean inwards, which is fine for a dramatic shot, but you can also step back as far as the surroundings allow to get a straighter, calmer view. Leaving plenty of sky around the tower helps it stand out. If you want a picture that shows the setting, include a little of the foreground, such as a few visitors for a sense of scale.

Take a few versions: one wide shot with the surroundings, one upright shot of the full height, and one closer detail of the structure against the sky. Check the official site before you go if you want to go up the tower, as access and opening arrangements can change.
text.geographic_location: Gyeongju Tower is in Gyeongju Expo Park, in Gyeongju, North Gyeongsang Province, South Korea. It was completed in 2007 along with the Gyeongju Expo Culture Center.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so check a map app for the route to Gyeongju Expo Park. The tower is 82 metres tall, so it should be easy to pick out once you are close. The phone icon on the map is at the tower itself, so there is no extra walk once you arrive. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) when you are close to the base and want the whole height in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) from further back for a more natural look. The telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) is useful for picking out details of the upper part of the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. For a fuller view of the whole structure, step back as far as the surroundings allow until the top fits in your frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn the phone upright and switch on the gridlines. Line the tower up with a vertical grid line so it looks straight, and leave some sky above the top. Keep your phone as level as you can for the first shot, then tilt it up for a dramatic angle.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the sky keeps its colour and the tower is not a dark shape. Use night mode after dark and hold the phone steady against a railing or your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters a tall structure, and a clear sky gives the cleanest background.

text.access_note: Gyeongju Expo Park is the setting, but entry to the tower itself may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.

Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters tall structures.

name: Poseokjeong
label: Poseokjeong Site
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '포석정지' (4 web pages); placed at our map tiles: '포석정' (pois).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q624306: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Abalone-shaped stream channel where Silla kings held banquets.

text.description: Poseokjeong was once the setting for a royal villa from the Unified Silla period, said to be the most beautiful of its time. The pavilion has gone, and what remains is a curved granite waterway set among trees on the slope below Namsan. That makes it a quiet, textured subject rather than a grand building. The channel is shaped like an abalone, which gives the site its name, and it is made up of 63 granite blocks. It was named Historic Site No. 1 in 1963, and the grounds cover 7,432 m². According to the history, noble guests once sat along the channel, floated cups of wine on the water and composed poetry. The site is also linked with the fall of the Silla kingdom, because King Gyeongae was killed here in the 920s. For photographs, the pleasure is in the curve of the stone against the zelkova, pine and bamboo, some of which are several hundred years old. It looks different in autumn foliage, with fallen leaves and with snow, so it changes a lot through the year. Keep the waterway as the main subject and let the trees fill the frame around it. There are no buildings left on the site, so you will not have to work around modern structures in the shot.
text.geographic_location: Poseokjeong is on the slope below Namsan in Gyeongju. It sits in wooded grounds near the foot of the mountain.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop is listed for this spot, so use a map app to route to Poseokjeong on the slope below Namsan. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the whole curve of the waterway with the trees behind it. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you need to stand close and still fit the channel in. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the joins between the stone blocks or fallen leaves lying in the channel.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (front (south) side of the granite waterway, the angle used in the official front-view photo). The curved, abalone-shaped granite waterway (about 22 m long) set among trees on the slope below Namsan, with no buildings left on the site.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the curve of the channel along one of the lower lines, so that it leads the eye into the picture. Keep the trees as a backdrop and leave a little ground in the foreground. Crouching slightly makes the stonework look more solid.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stone to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if bright leaves or sky are washing out the picture. In autumn, try a Live Photo to catch leaves moving. Take a few shots, since the light under the trees can change quickly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Autumn is best for the foliage around the waterway. Early morning is also suggested, as it is likely to be less crowded.

text.access_note: This is a designated historic site (Sajeok No. 1), so check the official site before you go for current opening times and any rules about entering the grounds.

name: Dabotap
label: Dabotap Pagoda
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/6227294715: the OpenStreetMap point 'Dabotap'.
notes: Ornate stone pagoda in the Bulguksa courtyard.

text.description:
Dabotap is a stone pagoda in the courtyard of Bulguksa temple in Gyeongju. It is the more decorated of the two pagodas that stand facing each other. When you come in over the Cheongun and Baegun Bridge, Dabotap is on the right and its plainer partner, Seokgatap, is on the left. Tradition says it was built in 751, in the reign of King Gyeongdeok of Silla. It is National Treasure no. 20 and stands 10.29 m tall, and its three storeys are carved in an ornate style. It has a staircase on each of its four sides, square pillars under the first roof, and an eight-sided upper section with a lotus carved with sixteen petals. Only one of the four stone lions that guarded the stairs is still in place. The pagoda also appears on the 10 won coin.

It photographs well because it is full of detail and sits on its own in an open courtyard. Take one full-height shot, then move in with zoom for the railings, roofs and lotus carving. If you want the story of the two pagodas, turn and include Seokgatap in a wider frame. Wait a moment for other visitors to move out of the shot, and keep your phone level so the pagoda does not lean.
text.geographic_location: Dabotap is inside the grounds of Bulguksa temple, in the main courtyard just past the Cheongun and Baegun Bridge. It stands on the right-hand side, facing Seokgatap.
text.directions_text: Head for Bulguksa temple in Gyeongju. Once you have entered over the Cheongun and Baegun Bridge, Dabotap is on your right. The phone icon on the map is about 20 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole pagoda from where you stand. Switch to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the carved roofs, railings and the lion. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the pagoda and part of the courtyard together, and keep it away from the edges of the frame, where it can stretch the shape.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 20 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. Keep to the visitor areas and do not climb on or lean over any railing.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line a vertical grid line up with the pagoda's centre so the sides stay straight. Leave a little sky above the top. Then take a second, tighter shot using zoom for the upper roofs and the lotus carving. For a third shot, include Seokgatap on the opposite side to show the pair.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the carved detail does not wash out. Take a few frames in case people walk through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually means softer light and fewer visitors. Midday sun can flatten the carving, so zoom in on details then.

text.access_note: Dabotap is inside Bulguksa, a working Buddhist temple, so check the official site before you go for entry and visiting rules.

label: Seokgatap Pagoda

text.description: Seokgatap is a plain, elegant stone pagoda in the grounds of Bulguksa temple in Gyeongju. It dates from the Silla period and probably from around 751, when the temple was completed. It stands 10.75 metres tall, directly across from its more ornate partner, Dabotap. The two make a striking pair: Dabotap is more elaborate, while Seokgatap is very simple. It has three storeys on a two-tier base, with no carvings on its faces, and the storeys step in at a steady 4:3:2 ratio that gives it a calm, balanced look. That clean shape is what makes it easy to photograph. It reads clearly as a single upright subject against the temple buildings and sky, and eight lotus-flower stones sit around it, which add a little foreground detail. Its fame also rests on what was found inside. During repairs in 1966, workers uncovered relics and a woodblock-printed Buddhist text, believed to be the oldest surviving printed material of its kind. For a good photo, stay at the edge of the courtyard and keep the whole pagoda in frame, vertical lines straight. Then take a second, wider shot that includes Dabotap or the roofline behind. Courtyards at temples can fill up, so be patient and wait for a gap between groups.
text.geographic_location: Seokgatap is in the courtyard of Bulguksa temple in Gyeongju. It stands opposite Dabotap.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for Bulguksa temple in Gyeongju. Once inside the temple grounds, go to the main courtyard, where Seokgatap and Dabotap face each other. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole pagoda. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the pagoda, Dabotap and the buildings in one frame, and keep the pagoda away from the edges, where it can stretch. Use telephoto (2x-5x) for the stepped roof edges and the lotus stones.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. This is very close, so you will probably need the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) or a few steps back to fit it in.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the pagoda up with a vertical line so it stands straight. Hold the phone level, as tilting upwards makes the sides lean. Try one shot centred to show the symmetry, then one with Dabotap in the edge of the frame to show the contrast between the pair.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the pagoda to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little if the sky is bright, so the stone keeps its detail. Take a few frames, as people often walk through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day or later in the afternoon is usually calmer and the light is softer. Midday light and crowds make it harder.

name: Bunhwangsa
label: Bunhwangsa Temple
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '분황사 모전석탑' (4 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/479216009: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Bunhwangsa Temple' (169 m across).
notes: Temple with the oldest brick-style stone pagoda in Korea.

text.description:
Bunhwangsa is a quiet Buddhist temple in Gyeongju, and its main attraction is a small, weathered stone pagoda. The temple is recorded as built in 634 under Queen Seondeok, and in the Silla period it was one of the kingdom's four main temples. The pagoda is National Treasure No. 30 and is described as the oldest dated pagoda from Silla. It is made of dark stone blocks cut to look like bricks. Only three tiers survive today, though old records say it once stood nine storeys high. Guardian figures flank the doorways on each side, and a stone lion sits at each corner of the low platform.

It photographs well because the pagoda is compact, has a strong shape, and sits in open temple grounds. In the right season, flower beds of cosmos or zinnias in front of it give you an easy foreground, with the temple buildings softening the background. The cosmos are usually out from about September to mid-October.

For a simple, clean picture, stand in front of the pagoda and keep the flowers low in the frame. Then step closer for details such as the guardian figures and the lions. If the pagoda looks crowded, try an early or late visit. For a second view, the bell pavilion in the grounds gives a quieter angle on the pagoda. You can also try the open ground of the nearby Hwangnyongsa site, where fields of barley (spring) or cosmos (autumn) stretch back toward the pagoda.
text.geographic_location: Bunhwangsa is in Gyeongju, close to the open site of the former Hwangnyongsa temple. The temple is part of the Gyeongju Historic Areas.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so check a map for the route from central Gyeongju to Bunhwangsa. The Hwangnyongsa site is nearby, so the two are easy to visit together. Once inside the temple grounds, the pagoda is the main feature and easy to find. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the pagoda with flowers in front. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the guardian figures, lions and stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Walk to the front of the pagoda (분황사 모전석탑) for the view. From there you see the three-tier stone pagoda with flower beds in front and the temple buildings behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the pagoda on one of the vertical lines, with the flower beds filling the bottom third. Crouch a little so the flowers sit in front of the stone. For a different view, try the bell pavilion in the temple grounds for a quieter angle, or the Hwangnyongsa site for the fields leading toward the pagoda.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the pagoda to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the dark stone keeps its detail and the sky does not turn white. In a busy moment, a Live Photo can help you pick a frame without other visitors.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and it is usually quieter. The flowers are seasonal: cosmos roughly September to mid-October, barley in the nearby fields in spring.

text.access_note: It is an active temple where photography is allowed, but please do not disturb monks or other visitors; check the official site before you go for current access details.
claims_not_in_sources: Modest dress and quiet behaviour are generally expected in a working temple.
Dark stone can lose detail against a bright sky, so lowering the exposure helps.

text.description:
Cheonwangmun Gate is a traditional gatehouse in Gyeongju, and it works well as a phone photo because a gate gives you a clear shape and an opening that leads the eye through to whatever lies beyond. Gates like this are made for symmetrical, front-on pictures. They also reward a slightly angled shot that shows the depth of the structure.

The phone icon on the map is about 70 m south of the subject. That distance helps. You can fit the whole building in the frame, with some ground in front and sky above, without tilting the phone upwards and leaning the walls inwards.

If there are details under the eaves, look at those, along with the texture of the materials and the way people pass through the opening. A person walking through gives a sense of scale, but wait for people to clear the frame if you want the gate on its own. Turn on gridlines to keep the roofline level, and check that the vertical edges look straight before you press the shutter.

Check access and entry rules before you go.
text.geographic_location: Cheonwangmun Gate is on the Gyeongju map, in the Gyeongju area.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop is listed close by, so start from Gyeongju town and go by taxi or hired scooter, giving the name Cheonwangmun Gate to the driver or your map app. The gate is 69 metres to the north of it, about 1 minute on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 70 m south of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the whole gate. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you cannot step back far enough, and use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details higher up on the gate.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 70 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. From here the whole gate fits in the frame with room to spare. Walk a few steps closer for tighter shots.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Centre the opening and use the gridlines to keep the roofline level, or step a little to one side for an angled view that shows the depth of the building. Keep a strip of ground at the bottom so the gate looks settled rather than cut off. Wait for people to clear the frame if there are any.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the gate to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the gate keeps its detail. Try a Live Photo to catch people passing through, but take a normal shot as well.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light. On an overcast day the colours often look richer and there are fewer harsh shadows.

text.description:
A pond is easy to photograph with a phone. The surface can act as a mirror, so you can fit the shoreline, the plants and the sky into one picture. On a calm day the reflection doubles the scene and makes a simple frame look more interesting.

The pond is about 83 metres to the north. Adjust the zoom to suit how much of the pond you want in the frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a natural view that looks like what you saw. If you want more of the shoreline or the sky, switch to the ultra-wide lens (0.5x). Keep the horizon level with the gridlines on, because a tilted water line is obvious in a pond picture.

If something on the far side catches your eye, try the 2x telephoto setting and let it fill the frame. Wait for ripples to settle before you take the shot. Tap the water or the far shore to focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly if the sky is washing out the colours. Take a few frames, moving slightly where access allows, since a small change in position can move the reflection a long way.
text.geographic_location: Banyayeonji Pond is on the Gyeongju map.
text.directions_text: Once you reach it, the pond lies about 83 metres to the north, roughly 1 minute on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 85 m south of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x). Switch to the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) for a wider sweep of water and sky. Use 2x telephoto for details on the far shore.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 85 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the water line on a gridline and keep it level. Include a little shoreline in the foreground so the picture has depth. Take one wide frame and one closer frame with 2x for variety.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the far shore to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is too bright. Wait for the water to settle, and try a Live Photo to catch the best moment.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Calm, soft light in the early morning or late afternoon usually gives the cleanest reflections and the least glare.

name: Hwangnyongsa
label: Hwangnyongsa Site
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '황룡사지' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: '사자봉' (pois).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q491548: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Huge ruined Silla temple site with foundation stones.

text.description: Hwangnyongsa was once the great state temple of the Silla kingdom, and today it is a wide, open field of stone foundations. Work began in 553 and the temple was finished in 644. Its nine-story wooden pagoda, reported at about 80 m tall, was among the tallest structures in East Asia until Mongol invasions burned it in 1238. Only the foundation stones remain, but they show the scale well. The walled area covered roughly 80,000 square metres, and the pagoda stood at the centre with halls on three sides. That layout is what makes the place photograph well. The low stone bases lead the eye across a big, uncluttered space, and the reconstructed pagoda model and the History and Culture Center give a backdrop. The close-up view is from among the pagoda foundations inside the site, facing along the central axis of the temple layout. Keep the stones in the foreground and let the open ground and the buildings beyond fill the rest of the frame. Please stay off the foundations, as climbing on them is not allowed. The planting around the ruins changes with the seasons (barley, cosmos, zinnias, or nothing), so colour varies through the year. For a second view, try the fields running from Bunhwangsa Temple towards the ruins, or the elevated outlook at the History and Culture Center.
text.geographic_location: Hwangnyongsa is in Gyeongju, on open ground close to the Bunhwangsa Temple and not far from the old Banwolseong palace site. The ruins sit on a plain surrounded by hills.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stop is listed for this spot. If you are visiting Bunhwangsa Temple, the ruins are about 140 m away. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole field of foundation stones, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the pagoda model or the History and Culture Center in the distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (among the pagoda foundations, facing the central axis of the temple layout). The stone foundations of the nine-story pagoda and the open ruins, with the reconstructed pagoda model and History and Culture Center beyond them. For the close-up view, walk in among the pagoda foundations and face along the central axis of the temple layout. Avoid stepping or climbing on the stones.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the horizon on the upper third line, with a large stone base in the lower third as your foreground. Crouch a little so the stones lead the eye towards the buildings behind. As an alternative, try the barley or flower fields stretching from Bunhwangsa Temple towards the ruins.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stones to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the sky keeps its colour and the stone keeps its detail. Try a panorama to show the full width of the site, moving the phone slowly and steadily.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning for fewer people and softer light, or late afternoon for warm light over the stones.

text.access_note: This is an open-air archaeological site where the grounds are generally open all day, but opening times may vary, so check the official site on the day before you go.
